speakeroldname: Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved:
speechtext: That Bill No. 19 to amend the Naturalization Act be now read a third time.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg to move,
seconded by Mr. Guthrie:
That the word "now" be left out, and the words "this day six months" be added to the end of the question.
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to address to the chamber any extended remarks in connection with this matter. We have considered the bill very fully in committee and also upon second reading. The fact is that in 1914 we enacted legislation with respect to naturalization, which legislation might be de-vided into two parts. The first part deals with the conditions under which applicants for naturalization may obtain British citizenship-no longer Canadian citizenship, but British citizenship. The second part deals with the procedure under which the Secretary of State satisfies himself that the conditions imposed with respect to qualifications have been observed by the applicant. The conditions under which applications are to be dealt with are: that the applicant should have resided in Canada for five years, should have a good character, should possess an adequate knowledge of English or French, and should have the intention of residing in the British dominions or remaining in the service of the crown. If those conditions are satisfied, and the Secretary of State is seized of sufficient information that those conditions have been complied with, the applicant is entitled, not as of right, but in the discretion of the Secretary of State, to British citizenship.
We differ with respect to the question of procedure. Heretofore in this country the procedure has been to leave the matter to the judges of the country. There is a provision in the present statute that unless there be grave reasons why it should not be so, the applicant should appear before a judge and satisfy him of his having complied with the conditions to which I have referred. These conditions with respect to procedure are now being swept away, and hereafter two persons,
who are natural-iborn British subjects, and a justice of the peace, who may not be, will certify to the Secretary of State that there has been compliance with the conditions under which citizenship could be obtained.
We object to these changes for two reasons. First, because no evidence has been adduced of any sufficient weight indicating that there has been any difficulty that should be considered sufficient by this parliament in the administration of the act as it now stands. In other words, there has been no crying grievance for which a remedy should be provided. Secondly, the minister himself, as well as the only judicial opinion to which he referred in the course of the debate on this matter, has made it abundantly dear that the department desired uniformity or, as Chief Justice Meredith said, the "even administration of the law." There being no evidence of any crying grievance on the part of anyone that could not be remedied by existing legislation, the first ground disappears.
With respect to the second, the method now proposed not only does not make for uniformity or convenience in the administration of the law, but permits a variation in the administration of the law, within an area of five miles, in dealing with two applicants. Entirely different standards are observed. That not only makes for inconvenience in the administration of the law and lack of uniformity, but it puts a premium on laxity in administration. For these reasons, without going into the details that have been traversed in committee, we deem it incumbent upon us to move that this bill do not receive the sanction of parliament and be enacted into law, but that it disappear from the order paper.
If there were any crying grievance in the law as it now stands, if the law were inadequate to deal with the difficulties that have been referred to, if it were shown that a new method would conduce to convenience and to uniformity in the administration of the law, or that the safeguards which should surround naturalization of aliens were any better than those that now exist, there would be no difficulty in acceding to the proposals now being advanced by the administration. But as the matter now stands we are asked to substitute, for the traditional fairness and discretion of the judiciary of this country, the discretion of two persons, perhaps illiterate, who may reside near the intending applicant, together with a justice of the peace who might not himself be able to speak the English language or to understand whether the applicant's knowledge of it was adequate or inadequate. For the discretion of the judiciary

Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinfret
we are asked to substitute a discretion such as that. Against that we protest, and for that reason we move the six months' hoist with respect to this legislation.

I do not desire to offer any extended remarks at this stage; I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) that the matter has been thoroughly discussed at one stage or another, either on the second reading or in committee. I merely wish to summarize now the main reasons for the changes we have proposed.
In 1911 at the imperial conference an agreement was reached between the representatives of the British government and those of the government of the dominions on certain enactments with relation to the granting of British citizenship throughout the empire. As has been pointed out during this discussion, it was required that an applicant should have resided five years within the British Empire and one year in that part of the empire wherein the application was filed; that he should be of good character; that he should possess a knowledge of one of the official languages of the dominion wherein the application was made; and that he should indicate his intention to reside within the British Empire in the future. These were the requirements that were made compulsory with respect to the granting of naturalization within any part of the empire. But the local regulations were left to the various legislatures or governments within the empire. The principle was laid down, however-and this is not disputed now-that absolute discretion should rest with the government in every dominion as to allowing or disallowing the granting of a certificate. The local procedure, as I have just said, was a matter for the individual government to determine.
In this country prior to 1914, when the present act was put on the statutes, applications for naturalization were filed and presented to the courts of the land, and I believe that in the act of 1914 that feature was retained in our legislation rather as a remnant of the past than as a new enactment. Since then it has been found-and the claim has been pressed upon the Department of the Secretary of State-that for a number of years there has been great inconvenience in the less settled parts of the country on the part of applicants desiring to be naturalized. They have found it difficult to appear in person before the judge. This difficulty has been amply illustrated in the debate that has taken place on this bill. We have tried to 
show that leaving it to the discretion of the individual judge to pass upon the requirements as to character or adequacy of knowledge does not make for uniformity in decision but tends rather to serious discrepancies.
I would point out that in no other dominion of the empire does the applicant appear before a judge. This is a provision that exists onlly in Canada. And, I repeat, it was carried into legislation in 1914 not so much as a new provision but rather as a remnant of the practice in the past in the granting of naturalization. During this debate we have been asked what would be substituted for the present procedure requiring appearance before the court and the decision of a judge. I have indicated what the regulations will be On this point some hon. members have expressed the opinion that there would be a greater safeguard and a greater guarantee if the regulations, instead of being merely departmental, were made statutory. The government at once yielded to that opinion, deeming it proper and just. We accepted it because we were very anxious to demonstrate to the house and to the country that we had not the least unworthy motive in the matter. For no consideration did we desire either to make naturalization something that could be obtained without a proper guarantee or, as some hon. members have suggested, to make use of it for any political or electoral purpose. For these reasons we at once yielded to the demand that the regulations be made statutory, and that is why we have embodied in the bill, now proposed for third reading, the provision regarding the posting of a copy of the application in 'the nearest post office, retaining as well the period of ninety days which is now in the act. This body, I may point out here, is no longer local or territorial in character; it is now a national institution operating throughout the country and giving magnificent results.
I do not think I need stress these points any longer. I have spoken on many occasions in the course of this debate and have done my best to explain the policy of the government and to indicate the intentions of the depart-

ment in the matter, and I ask the house to pass the third reading of the bill, which will vest in tihe government the power of allowing or disallowing the granting of a certificate of naturalization, Which we claim is a matter of policy and not a matter of a judicial nature. This legislation will bring our act into perfect conformity with the statutes in other parts of the empire. We make our regulations statutory, following the practice which exists in other dominions, and by doing away with the inconvenience to the applicants of appearing in person before the courts, after which they must wait for a period of months before receiving their certificate, the government will be enabled within a reasonable time and under perfect guarantees and. safeguards to grant certificates of naturalization to immigrants who have legally entered this country and have resided here in a peaceful and law-abiding way for five years. I think every hon. member will agree that if we want to build up this country and if we want to make Canada prosperous and progressive it will not suffice to invite immigrants from all parts of the world to settle in this country; it will not be sufficient to open our doors to these immigrants. After they have lived here for a number of years, after they have shown themselves to be of good character and have learned one of our official languages we should bind them to this country by making it possible for every one of them to receive the priceless gift of British citizenship.

Sir EUGENE FISET (Rimouski) moved the third reading of Bill 17 respecting the St. John River Storage Company.

Mr. Speaker, I move seconded by Mr. Woods-worth:
That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada, in accordance with the Revised Statutes of Canada 1927, chapter 35, section 56, in order that the constitutional question therein involved may be given a legal interpretation.
This bill involves several most important questions of law, and -to elucidate those questions I think it welll to state some -matters of fact. I would draw the attention of the house to -page 5 of the bill, where will be found the preamble of -chapter 100 of the statutes of Quebec, 1927, which we are called upon to adopt and confirm by this bill. The first paragraph reads thus:
Whereas the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission Company has, by its petition, represented:-
That it was incorporated by the Act 15 George V, chapter 117, for the purpose of regulating the flow of the waters in the Madawaska and St. Francis rivers, constructing certain dams for the storage of water, and other incidental powers required for the purpose of carrying on the development of the water-power at Grand Falls, in the province of New Brunswick.
It will be observed that this paragraph recites that the act of 15 George V, -chapter 117, was passed to enable certain dams for the storage of water to be constructed. This I will deal with later on. The work was to be

St. John River Storage Company
undertaken, by the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission Company. The second paragraph of the preamble is as follows:
That arrangements have now been made whereby the development of the water-power at Grand Falls is to be undertaken and carried out by the Saint John River Power Company, a company incorporated by the Act 16 George V, chapter 45, of the acts of the legislature of the province of New Brunswick.
The .third paragraph is in these words:
That the lieutenant-governor in council of New Brunswick and the New Brunswick Electric Powrer Commission, with the approval of the said lieutenant-governor in council, were, by the terms of the said act, authorized to transfer or otherwise render available to the Saint John River Power Company all property, rights, powers and privileges vested in the province or in the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission-
The same concern.
-which the company might deem necessary or useful for or in connection with the development and generation of hydro-electric power or energy at Grand Falls and pondage and storage thereof in New Brunswick or beyond its borders,-
"Beyond its borders" is most important.
-and, without limitation of the generality of the foregoing, all rights, powers and privileges of the province of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission under or by virtue of the Act 15, George V, chapter 117, incorporating the company petitioner, and any and all other property and rights acquired for the development of storage in the province of Quebec.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, the province of New Brunswick decided to embark on two big undertakings. T'he first had to do with the development of hydro-electric power at Grand Falls on the St. John river; the second was for the purpose of constructing certain works in the province of Quebec to regulate the flow of the Madawaska and St. Francis rivers in connection with <the water-power development at Grand Falls. It will be noted that the new Brunswick Electric Power Commission Company, although incorporated by the province of Quebec and also by the province of New Brunswick, forms one single body, acting for and on behalf of the province of New Brunswick. Projected as a public ownership undertaking, after a change of government the legislature of New Brunswick empowered the new government to sell to a private company all the rights belonging to the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission. It ceased to be a public utility concern and became a private company. What sort of company? It is a branch of the International Paper Company, and if hon. members will look at page 258 of the New Brunswick statutes of 1926 they will .see the name
of that well known financier, Mr. Archibald Graustein, manufacturer of Framingham, Massachusetts, who is the head of the International Paper Company. But a distinction must be made between the province of New Brunswick on the one hand and that gentleman on the other. When the province of New Brunswick sold its rights to a private individual there was a transfer, according to the preamble of the act, of all rights, powers and privileges vested in the province or in the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission:
Which the company might deem necessary or useful for or in connection with the development and generation of hydro-electric power or energy at Grand Falls and pondage and storage thereof in New Brunswick or beyond its borders, and, without limitation of the generality of the foregoing, all rights, powers and privileges of the province and of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission under or by virtue of the Act 15, George V, chapter 117.
The acts which we are now called upon to confirm contradict themselves. In the preamble to the second act. we see that the province of New Brunswick has no longer any rights. I say that as a lawyer and without prejudice, because I am not now discussing the legal aspect of the question. My first wish is to make a statement of the facts according to this official document which we have in our hands. The moment the second Quebec bill was passed in 1927 the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission ceased to have any rights. The province of New Brunswick no longer had rights either in the power or in the storage; those rights were all transferred in virtue of the act of the New Brunswick legislature.
Another paragraph of the preamble to which I wish to direct the attention of the house is the following:
That in order to make fully effective such change of enjoyment of the benefits of the act incorporating the petitioner and to render the same effective for the purpose intended, and to change the name of the company, it is necessary that the said act be amended.
It was two years after the first act was passed, and one year after the transfer of the rights of the province of New Brunswick and of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission to a private company, that another Quebec act was passed, "to make fully effective such change of enjoyment of the benefits of the act". I believe the deed of sale was completed, but the St. John River Storage Company was not a party to the sale. What I find strange is this. After the province of New Brunswick had sold all its rights to< a private company there were no more rights

St. John River Storage Company
that could be enjoyed, no more rights from which there were benefits; yet an act was passed1 in Quebec "to make fully effective such change". At that moment the former directors of the New Brunswick Power Commission, incorporated by the Quebec act, ceased to act for the province of New Brunswick. A change of government had taken place; they were no longer representing the province. And, I may add, they had not been incorporated alone; their successors also had been incorporated under the same name of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission. And their successors, according to the Quebec act, were to be replaced by the lieutenant governor of the province of New Brunswick. The first three directors of the company, incorporated by the first act, were incorporated not in their private capacity but in their official capacity as representatives of the executive of New Brunswick. I am ready to believe that they had no personal interest in the matter; and it could not be otherwise, because everyone in this house knows that no member of the executive can have any personal interest with the executive. Such persons can act only in their public capacity. If therefore they had had a private interest-which I cannot believe -it would have been strictly illegal and against the general principles of government, not only in Canada but in every other democratic country.
After that change of government, when the three gentlemen were defeated who are named in section 1 of the first act, chapter 117 of the Quebec statutes of 1925, those gentlemen no longer had any right to speak for the executive of the province of New Brunswick. The only three gentlemen who are named in this bill-named in both acts, according to schedule A-are:
The Hon. Pierre J. Veniot, of the town of Bathurst, in the county of Gloucester, in the province of New Brunswick, premier of the province of New Brunswick, the Hon. Ernest A. Smith, of the town of Shediac, in the county of Westmorland, in the province of New Brunswick, chairman of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, and the Hon. Joseph Enoil Michaud, of the town of Edmunds-ton, in the county of Madawaska, in the province of New Brunswick, member of the executive council of the said province of New Brunswick, and a commissioner of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission.
They are the three gentlemen mentioned in section 1 of the first Quebec act; and according to section 4, to which I alluded a moment ago, the persons named in section 1 of the act shall be the first directors and shall remain in office as such until replaced by the lieutenant governor in council of the province

of New Brunswick. That section has been changed in the second bill, and now reads as follows:
The persons named in section 1 of this act shall be the first members and directors, and their successors in office at the date of this amendment shall remain in office as such until the election of their successors in accordance with the provisions of the Quebec Companies Act.
When the second bill was passed at Quebec the gentlemen who were mentioned in the first bill were no longer acting for the province of New Brunswick, and even if there had been no change after the general election they would have had no power to act for that province because at that moment New Brunswick had sold all its rights in the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission to a private company. The same thing cannot be sold twice, or to two different people; they had sold their rights and had nothing left.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to a very delicate question. I have the greatest regard for the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot); I believe he is an honest man; I believe in his sincerity and integrity, and because I so believe I cannot think he has any interest in the matter. If he had an interest in it I would say that I have no more confidence in him, and I believe the people of the country would say the same. If the Postmaster General has no private interest in this matter I will appeal to my friends on this side of the house to divide equally, in order not to displease my friend from Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset); I will ask the support of my hon. friends opposite, and that will give me a nice majority. At any rate, I have explained the facts as shortly as possible in order to acquaint the house with the question now before it.
Here we have two Quebec bills coming before us for approval and adoption. Are they legal? Are they intra vires? Or on the other hand are they illegal and ultra vires? If they are illegal can we make them any better by adopting and confirming them? This is not only a matter of interest to the county of Temiseouata which I have the honour to represent in this house and in which this proposed storage plant will be built, involving the flooding of about forty square miles of farm land, as a lawyer for one of the companies interested in this matter told me on Sunday last; this is not only a matter of interest to that county but it is a matter of interest to the country at large.

St. John River Storage Company
We should know the jurisdiction of this parliament and of the provincial legislatures in order that we may not exceed that jurisdiction, and before any measure is passed we should ascertain whether or not we have sufficient authority to so deal with it. In connection with this matter I represent my county under a special power of attorney, contained in a resolution passed by the county council of Temiscouata some time ago. I do not wish to hurt the feelings of anyone; I think this matter should be considered from a broad point of view; it should be considered without favouritism and without any suggestion of friendship or enmity. If it is good this house should pass it, and I am sure that if the house finds it to be bad the amendment will be adopted and the matter referred to the supreme court for interpretation.
Section 1 of this bill reads as follows:
In so far as the parliament of Canada has authority so to do the two acts of the legislature of the province of Quebec, set forth in schedule "A" to this act, are hereby adopted and confirmed, to the same extent as if re* enacted herein.
That reminds me of the labels we sometimes see, bearing the words, "Glass. Fragile. Handle with care." This section clearly shows that the promoters of the bill know it is illegal. Under the British North America Act the imperial parliament delegated authority to the Dominion parliament and provincial legislatures of Canada to enact laws, and duly fixed the limits of their respective jurisdictions. Such is the constitution of this country, drafted by those statesmen who are rightly called the fathers of confederation, and later adopted by the Imperial parliament. As it now stands, that act cannot be changed by the Dominion or Imperial parliaments except by and with the unanimous consent of the provinces, who were a party to that agreement. Moreover, the rights and powers conferred upon the Dominion parliament by the Imperial parliament cannot be delegated to the provincial legislatures, or vice versa. The Dominion parliament is bound to act within the limits of its own jurisdiction as defined and determined by the British North America Act, and those limits may not and cannot be exceeded. The same rule undoubtedly applies to the provincial legislatures, and when the Dominion parliament or any provincial legislature exceeds in its enactments the limits fixed by the British North America Act, such enactments are ultra vires and null and void, because of the lack of
authority possessed by the legislative body. These are fundamental and elementary rules of constitutional law.
To sum up, no legislative body can confer upon anyone rights or privileges which it does not possess.. Part VI of the British North America ActJ entitled "Distribution of legislative powers'", contains the following disposition under the subtitle "Exclusive Powers of Provincial Legislatures." Section 92 of the act reads thus:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say,-
10.	Local works and undertakings, other than such as are of the following classes:-
(a)	Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province;
11.	The incorporation of companies with provincial objects.
Both the above-mentioned provisions 3hall be construed with the last paragraph of section 91, which enumerates the powers of parliament, and which reads as follows:
And any matter coming within any of the c'asses of subjects enumerated in this section shall not be deemed to come within the class of matters of a local or private nature comprised in the enumeration of the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces.
Such are the limits fixed by the imperial parliament for the respective jurisdiction of this parliament and of the provincial legislatures with regard to incorporation of companies. One should note that the words "exclusive" and "exclusively" have been intentionally repeated to clear any possible doubt on the legislator's intent and also to remove all conflicts of jurisdiction. What interpretation has been given by the fathers of confederation to that part of our constitution? In the legislative assembly on February 6, 1865, the Attorney General, Sir John A. Macdonald said:
Any hon. member on examining the list of different subjects which arc to be assigned to the general and local legislatures respectively, will see that all the great questions which affect the general interests of the confederacy as a whole, are confided to the federal parliament, while the local interests and local laws of each section are preserved intact, and entrusted to the care of the local bodies.
It will be seen that the local legislatures have the control of all local w-orks; and it is a matter of great importance, and one of the chief advantages of the federal union and of local legislatures, that each province will have the power and means of developing its own resources and aiding its own progress after its own fashion and in its own way. Therefore all the local improvements, all local enterprises or undertakings of any kind, have been left to
Time.

Was the legislature of the province of Quebec empowered with jurisdiction or authority to incorporate by section 1 of chapter 117 of the statutes of Quebec the first members and directors of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission Company in their official capacity as representatives of the executive of another province? Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this amendment I may say that it is not my intention to deal with the legal aspect of it, but may I call the attention of the committee to this fact, that the Quebec legislature passed two acts touching the franchise which was granted to New Brunswick and later to the company in question? One act was passed in 1925 and the other in 1927, and if either of those acts were considered by my hon. friend ultra vires of the province of Quebec, there has been sufficient time to apply to the Dominion government for a veto. No such application has been made.
I wish at this point to give a history of the question so that hon. members may be seized of all the facts and be placed in a position to vote intelligently upon the amend-50103-181J
ment. In 1925, the province of New Brunswick, of which I had the honour at that time of being premier, adopted a policy of hydro development by public ownership. An act incorporating myself as premier, the chairman of the New Brunswick hydro commission and one of the commissioners was passed by the province of New Brunswick. An application was then made to the province of Qudbec to incorporate the company so that they could hold property and franchises in the name of one province, namely, New Brunswick, in another province, namely, Quebec. The reason for that was this. The development was to take place and the dam to be built at Grand Falls on the river St. John which, at a point two and a half miles above this site, forms the international boundary between the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine. The water flowing in the international river was not sufficient to warrant the expenditure of a large sum of money at Grand Falls to develop 50,000 or 60,000 horse-power, without privileges being obtained either in the state of Maine on the Fish river or in Quebec at the Temiseouata lake. The matter was brought before the International Joint Commission and after that question was settled and the International Joint Commission reached a decision on all matters pertaining to the international waters, we made application to the authorities of the state of Maine for the privilege of damming what is known as the Fraser river and its ten lakes emptying into that river. That privilege we did not obtain.
We then applied to the province of Quebec for the privilege of damming the Temis-couata lake where it empties into the river whose waters flow into the St. John river at Edmundston. That privilege was granted on certain conditions, one of them being that the province of New Brunswick was to reserve for the use of the province of Quebec 5.000 horse-power to be delivered at the boundary between the two provinces at the will and call of the government of Quebec, they to do what they liked with it after it was delivered at the boundary. We entered into that agreement and the province of Quebec passed the first act in 1925. It is true, as my hon. friend says, that the government which had propounded the policy of public ownership was defeated, but I cannot admit with him that the government was defeated on that question alone. After the new government came into power and after considerable deliberation on their part, they decided to change the policy, and pass the franchise

St. John River Storage Company
to a company. Those rights were never sold as he wished the house to infer they were. They passed the franchise to this company for the development of Grand Falls under certain conditions. Among other conditions there was this, that they would enter into a contract with Frasers, Limited, for 13,000 dependable horse-power and 7,000 seasonal horse-power to be used by Frasers, Limited, for the establishment of a new pulp and paper mill on the north shore at or near Campbell-ton, a distance of 110 miles from Grand Falls across the province. The company to which was transferred this franchise by the local government also undertook as their part of the bargain to establish a new pulp mill on the north shore of New Brunswick either at Campbellton or at Dalhousie. It was also a condition of obtaining the franchise that the company should reserve six thousand horse-power for the absolute use of the New Brunswick hydro commission, which was then operating at Musquash. Those are the conditions under which the government coming into power in 1926 changed its policy of public ownership. This company under those conditions, under the franchise granted, began construction operations at Grand Falls in 1927, and to-day those operations have been completed, and they are prepared to distribute 50,000 horse-power throughout certain sections of the province of New Brunswick, but they cannot distribute that 50,000 horse-power unless the power as conferred upon them under the franchise granted by the government of the province of Quebec shall be left intact. That being so, they will go on with the construction- of a dam at the foot of Temiseouata lake. The construction of that dam will not overflow 40,000 acres of land, as my hon. friend says. He is getting his information from somebody who does not know what he is talking about. The survey of Temiseouata lake and of all that country was made under the direction of myself, then Premier of New Brunswick and Minister of Public Works for the province. The construction of that dam will raise the level of the lakes seven and one-half feet. It will not, according to engineering reports, cause any undue damage to land under cultivation in that country, but should such be the case the owners of that land are protected under the act, and damages, of course, will have to be paid.
My friend in his remarks said that he did not wish to hurt the feelings of anybody, and that he hoped he would not be hurting my feelings, because he felt that. speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
I was asked to second this amendment, and I did so solely on the character of the bill itself. I am not a lawyer, but I do not think that even a layman can read this bill without recognizing that it is most peculiar in its framing. I know nothing of the details of the situation in Quebec and New Brunswick other than what has been given to us by the mover of this amendment and by the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), but I must say that the explanation given by the Postmaster General has not made me feel that I made any mistake in seconding an amendment of this character.
As I have listened to the presentation of the argument in support of the amendment, it has struck me that the object of the bill is really to secure succession rights for an illegitimate still-born child. I am trying to put into ordinary phraseology what my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has conveyed in a very exhaustive and elaborate and learned discourse. I say a still-born child because the original company really never came into existence, never had life given to it. It was a public commission, and the effort is to try to give whatever rights it had to somebody else-to a private company. I would say that the child is illegitimate because evidently, if these rights were firmly established, the promoters of this bill would not be coming to us to-night. Apparently this is an elaborate, if somewhat clumsy, scheme by which, through collusion, the purposes of the British North America Act may be defeated.
I am not going into the question of public ownership versus private. Some of us believe in public ownership, but I do not think we need discuss that matter to-night. The Postmaster General has outlined the general background of the bill. Evidently an attempt was made by the province of Quebec to pass legislation incorporating the company. That legislation apparently is not intra vires. If it
is, we would not have this bill presented here.
Now, let me very briefly call attention tc two clauses of the bill. They are very simple I am leaving out the preamble. It may very well be made out from the legal standpoint that the present company seeking incorporatior is not the original company, but I suppose that is a matter between the two provinces concerned, and I do not know whether we ought to ask the Dominion authorities to interfere with that aspect of the case. Section 1 reads:
1. In so far as the parliament of Canada has authority so to do the two acts of the legislature of the province of Quebec, set forth in schedule "A" to this act, are hereby adopted and confirmed, to the same extent as if reenacted herein.
It does strike me, Mr. Speaker, that that is most peculiar phraseology. The bill contains two schedules. We have no right whatever to amend these schedules; we can only accept or reject them. So a bill is presented to us which really we have no right to amend. I think there was very good reason for pushing this bill through the committee stage last night, since the committee could not have changed a single clause. In dealing with this matter we are simply passing a piece of enabling legislation. The opening phrase of the section which I have quoted is very strange:
In so far as the parliament of Canada has authority so to do-
I do not like to be a party to passing legislation of that kind. Either we have authority or we have not, and we ought not to act in this conditional fashion. Then the second clause:
Notwithstanding the provisions of section one of this act,-
Which we were supposed just now to pass, -the company shall be governed by the applicable provisions of the Quebec Companies Act,-*
Evidently the legislature of Quebec had not the power to pass the legislation which it enacted, and now the promoters come to this parliament to legitimize their offspring. The scheme is that once we have legitimized the offspring, we are to turn it back to the province of Quebec, which will then exercise jurisdiction over it. Let me repeat, either we have jurisdiction or we have. not. Either the province of Quebec has jurisdiction or it has not. I take it that had it full jurisdiction this bill would not be before us. If we have jurisdiction, we have no right to resign our powers of administration to somebody else.
I think of the closely parallel case in my own province in which the province of Ontario was concerned. We have water powers in the Winnipeg river, the head waters of which and of the English river are in the province
2854	COMMONS
St. John River Storage Company
of Ontario. Several years ago an effort was made to establish storage dams at Lae Seul in the province of Ontario in order that the flow of water might be regulated and increased for the benefit of Manitoba. What was done? The right thing. Mr. Meighen, then Prime Minister, introduced legislation in this house which declared the works in Ontario to be for the general advantage of Canada, and as such they came under the federal jurisdiction, and they have been under that jurisdiction ever since, notwithstanding some attempt to repeal the legislation. Then the water-powers were developed under the Dominion authority. Now it strikes me the proper thing in this instance would have been for the province of New Brunswick to have come to the federal authorities and asked that -the works in Quebec be declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. Had that course been taken we would have been able to make suitable provision.
Was not that part of the water flowing through Manitoba under the jurisdiction of the federal government? It was not owned or controlled by the government of Manitoba.
That may have been one reason,-
The two eases are entirely different.

-but that does not affect my argument, because clearly under the British North America Act any such work an this may be declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. Suppose that in Manitoba we had control of our own natural resources, and -suppose we made a bargain with regard to Boundary falls, we will say, situated within the province of Ontario, can you imagine the Ontario authorities remaining quiescent? Not at all. Undoubtedly if we have the right to legislate in this case, it is because we control navigable streams, and I submit the proper course would have been to declare this work to be for the general advantage of Canada. Then it would have been carried out under the jurisdiction of the federal authority. Section 2 seeks to put the company back under the control of the province of Quebec. Again I submit that that is not in keeping with the spirit of the British North America Act.
Since this is an exceedingly complicated question, involving as it does the jurisdiction of the province of New Brunswick in which the works are actually situated, the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec in which the storage basin is located, and the jurisdiction of the
fMr. Woods worth.]
Dominion in so far as these are navigable streams, and as this work might well be declared for the general advantage of Canada, it seems to me that under these circumstances, and in order to remove all the constitutional difficulties, we might well have the matter referred to the supreme court for decision. This would cause a few months delay, but it would straighten out the tangle, and would not create the precedent that might be created by the passage of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, it is of vital importance to preserve the water powers of this country for the people. That part of the province of Quebec bordering on the province of New Brunswick is rich in water-powers. Those water-powers should not be alienated by parliament without good reason. The great principle of public ownership is involved in this bill. If the principle of this bill, which it is sought to apply to New Brunswick and to Quebec, had been applied to Ontario, there would have been no hydro-electric movement in this province, and instead of the two-cent unit we would now have a ten or twelve-cent unit.. This particular company is nothing but a subsidiary of the International Paper Company, which is tied up more or less with some fifteen or twenty corporations in Ontario and Quebec and in the United States, all parts of the great electrical merger, which is one of the most powerful trusts across the line.
This is a most dangerous bill, for many reasons. It is a most extraordinary bill, for it is proposed to make it retroactive, which is something that has never been done before by this parliament. Bill No. 17 is a most extraordinary measure. This parliament is called upon to give retroactive power to privincial enactments by adopting and confirming them. There are doubts expressed in the bill itself about the authority or jurisdiction of this parliament. If we have authority, the provincial legislatures have none; if, on the contrary, the provincial legislatures have authority we have none, and it is absolutely impossible for us not only to adopt and confirm but even to consider such provincial enactments. If they are ultra vires they cannot be confirmed; if they are intra vires we are deprived of jurisdiction or authority in the matter.
I do not care what political party takes up this question of water-power, whether it be the Liberal party or the Conservative party: I submit that it has no right to commit this country to private ownership. We must remember what was the condition of affairs in Ontario around 1900 and 1905. It was pretty much the same in Ontario at that time as it

St. John River Storage Company
is in Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia to-day. The Ross government had given away al the water-powers of the Niagara river to private ownership and there remained about 10.000-horse-power. In 1905 Sir James Whitney was returned to power and he cancelled the last orders in council with the result that the hydro-electric was instituted in Ontario.
The rights of various private companies were taken over on a fair basis, and the province was given a chance to develop its own waterpower. The result is that to-day we have cheap light and power in Ontario. That was a lesson to the people of New Brunswick, but it does not seem to have been taken to heart. I have read reports of surveys made in the province of New Brunswick and the province is admirably adapted to cheap electrical power. Unfortunately however that province has given away all its resources to private ownership, just as the province of Nova Scotia has done. The Liberal party in that province, in power for thirty-four years, handed over to private ownership the magnificent resources of the province including water-powers, fisheries, timber and mines. What was the result? The province became stagnant and' lost its population. There was no industrial growth, for the simple reason that he who has the key to the development of the water-powers of any country has the key to the future industrial development of that country.
I say therefore that the principle of this bill is wrong. It is unsound from a legal standpoint. But on grounds of public policy it is outrageous. We have no power to amend an act of the Quebec legislature and to hand over a public utility to private ownership. The gentlemen named in the bill as directors were appointed to act in an official capacity on behalf of the province of New Brunswick, so that the Postmaster General Mr. Veniot) and those associated with him in that capacity could have no individual interest in the matter. The gentlemen named in the bill are, first, the premier of the province, secondly, the chairman of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, and, thirdly, a member of the executive council of the province of New Brunswick, a commissioner of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission.
And their successors.

In Ontario the chairman of the commission was a member of the provincial cabinet, Sir Adam Beck, and the two other commissioners were nominated by the executive council; and they were appointed to act not in any private capacity but as public officials in order to preserve the water-powers of the province so as to provide the people with that boon of cheap light and power.
I regret very much indeed that the Conservative party has not seen fit to emulate the noble and inspiring example of Sir James Whitney in Ontario. At the coming election it would do that .party a great deal of good if the policy followed in Ontario in regard to water-powers were adopted not only in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia but also in British Columbia, a province which gives great promise for the future. That province, if given a chance, will go ahead by leaps and bounds. Everyone is proud of its growth and, I repeat, it would be an excellent thing for British Columbia and for the maritime provinces as well if the Conservatives would only follow the policy adopted in Ontario. If they did so they would reap a greater advantage in one day than they have been able to derive in all these years under private ownership.
I desire .to quote some prophetic words of the late President Roosevelt in regard to a similar situation which arose in his own country when he was in power. In regard to the waste of water-power in the United States he predicted that the day was not far distant when that country would run out of coal and other natural resources, particularly petroleum and gas. He said:
The people of our country are threatened by a monopoly more powerful than has been ever seen, as it affects very closely their domestic and industrial life. Our next generation will witness a shortage of those natural resources, petroleum and gas. The price of coal will be such that hydraulic power turned into electrical energy will, owing to its cost, become the prevailing factor for transport, for manufacturers, for lighting and heating our towns. Our hydraulic power alone, entirely and judiciously employed, would be adequate for the present needs of transport, industries, municipalities and private individuals. The major portion of these powers is not developed and remains the national property. It would be madness to part, without conditions, with one of our greatest resources. If we become guilty of this crime, our children will be bound to pay an annual royalty on a capitalization fixed at the highest price that the trade will stand for. They will see themselves struggling with powerful sweaters entrenched behind the doctrine of discharged rights strengthened by all means of protection that money can buy and the cunning of corporations defended by legal men. These ogres of finance will have succeeded long before then to monopolize those resources so as to be able to dictate to the people the management of their affairs and their way of existence. Public opinion will be their least worry.
These were the words of a prophetic statesman. In conclusion I have to say: American capitalists have found Canada a happy hunting ground. In the maritime provinces, in Quebec, Northern Ontario and the northwest, they have seized the water-powers which should be developed under public control. We find Mr. Backus getting control of the water-

St. John River Storage Company
powers in the northern section of new Ontario, and in addition to these magnificent rights and privileges he is given what virtually is a principality of timber as well. It will be a sorry day for the province of New Brunswick when they hand over their resources to any private monopoly. The province of Ontario spent a good deal of money for cheap light and power, but if we obtained that light and power from private companies it would have cost us many millions more to pay for the over-capitalization of these companies. When you pay for hydro power to-day you pay the actual cost of generating and distributing that power, but when you buy bread, milk, and many other things you have to pay a price which will return a profit on the millions of dollars invested of split common stock of no par value. I 'hope this legislation will not pass, and I intend to oppose it; I think we are on dangerous legal ground. I think we should not change this act of 1925 which incorporated certain gentlemen in their official capacities to operate a great public utility on the border of [DOT]these two provinces for the public good rather than for private gain.

I wish to offer just a few remarks on the question now before the house, and I am sorry I must differ with the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church). We are both supporters of public ownership in the province of Ontario, but this bill affects the provinces of New Brunswick and Quebec, and it must not be forgotten that the province of Quebec has always supported private ownership. That province has seen fit to legislate in regard to this matter at the instance of the province of New Brunswick, and I take it that when this proposition was first started the province of New Brunswick intended to establish a public ownership enterprise under the direction of the present Postmaster General of this government, who was then premier of that province. To-day someone else holds power there, and they have seen fit to change the position of the matter, apparently preferring private ownership. That is a matter quite within the rights of the province of New Brunswick, and I do not see why we should interfere in any way. These two provinces undertook to pass legislation of this kind in connection with their natural resources, and it would appear now that there is some doubt as to the validity of that legislation since these waters are interprovincial.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) referred to a case involving the provinces of Manitoba and Ontario, but these two provinces are in a very different position. Ontario is in possession of its own natural resources while Manitoba is not, so the jurisdiction of this parliament must prevail. That is why that legislation was passed in this house. This legislation does not imply that the province of Quebec or the province of New Brunswick have not power to deal with this matter; the fact is that there may be some feature in connection with the fact that these are interprovincial waters which may require the consent of this parliament, and as I understand it we are asked to deal with it on that basis. I dio not know of any reason why we should not allow the province of New Brunswick look after its own industries according to its own ideas. I would not wish to force my opinion or those prevailing in Ontario on the people of New Brunswick; this is within their jurisdiction and they should be left free to exercise their judgment in the matter. In my opinion this legislation is drawn very carefully, with all due respect to the member for Winnipeg North 'Centre. We simply grant such power as we possess in order to make this legislation more effective.
Might I ask my hon. friend a question? Has he read the bill of 1927 which appears in schedule A?
I have just read the material before me.
Des my hon. friend know who are the present directors of the St. John River Storage Company, and if so, are they acting in their private capacity or for the province of New Brunswick?

I am not very much interested in that. The province of Quebec has seen fit to continue its legislation and to pass an order in council consenting to the transfer of whatever rights are affected by this legislation. I think the government and the legal advisers of the province of Quebec are quite capable of looking after their own interests.
Is that order in council mentioned in the schedule?

It is referred to in the bill. I have never seen the order in council but it is referred to in this bill, and I am satisfied that no government would pass such an order in council unless it were satisfied it had the power to do so.

The house resumed, from May 8, consideration in committee of Bill No. 59, to incor-corporate the Federal Loan Company (as amended, and recommending that the title be changed to "An Act to incorporate the Federal Lending Company")-Mr. Lang- Mr. Johnston in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the bill was last before the committee, all sections had been adopted with the exception of section 5.
On section 5-Objects.

When this bill was
before the committee the other night the mover was not present. When clause 5 came up, a question was asked with regard to paragraph (b) which reads:
Notwithstanding anything contained in the Interest Act, and the Money Lenders Act, and in section 63 (c) of the Loan Companies Act.

Federal Loan Company
Information was requested why this company should be exempted from those acts. I should like to ask the mover of the bill for an explanation.

The company proposes to
lend, mainly on personal security, but also on mortgages, its own capital only. The bill prohibits the taking of deposits or the issue of debentures.	The company in lending
money on personal security will impose a loan charge in addition to a stipulated rate of interest and, in the case of small loans, the combined interest will exceed the limitations imposed by the Interest Act and the Money Lenders Act. These acts are therefore overridden by this bill. The section respecting interest which is overridden, and in regard to which a question was asked by my hon. friend a moment ago, reads:
Except as to mortgages on real estate, whenever any interest is, by the terms of any written or printed contract, W'hether under seal or not. made payable at a rate of percentage per day, week, month, or at any rate or percentage for any period less than a year, no interest exceeding the rate or percentage of five per centum per annum shall be chargeable, payable or recoverable on any part of the principal money unless the contract contains an express statement of the yearly rate or percentage of interest to which such other rate or percentage is equivalent.
That section is done away with by this bill, because the loan is going to be made on personal security mainly, but also on second mortgages or securities such as would not be accepted by the banks or loan companies. Therefore, in order to take care of the further risk, they are being withdrawn from the operation of these provisions. Then certain provisions have been incorporated in the bill from the Loan Companies Act. I may say that all these provisions have been gone into thoroughly by the Superintendent of Insurance and have his approval. We believe that this bill will result in a great deal of good in different parts of Canada in allowing men and women who sometimes find it necessary to raise money quickly upon securities that the banks and loan companies will not accept to get assistance without going to sharks and money leaders who will charge extortionate rates of interest. Believing that the bill is a good one, we confidently ask for the support of the house in passing it.
Does the exemption of this company from the operation of these acts mean that they will be allowed to charge just as high rates of interest as they can get?

No. They are allowed to charge a 6 per cent discount interest in making the
loan, and also after the loan is made a small charge, an investigation charge, which is regulated by the bill and depends upon the size of the loan, so that altogether the interest and charges may run up to as high as twelve or fourteen per cent, but that gets them by where they could not get by if they applied to a bank or loan company for a loan.

Is that the only charge
they are permitted to make?
Yes, that and the 6 per cent discount, which is paid weekly or monthly according to the provisions of the note itself.

I might add a word of explanation in regard to this bill, which was gone into very thoroughly by the committee in view of the fact that the bill embodied a new principle so far as we in Canada are concerned. This bill follows very closely along the lines of the Morris system which has been operated successfully in the United States.
Successfully for the borrower or the lender?

For both. They have found it to work very satisfactorily for a number of years. I believe that this bill will fill a want particularly in the larger centres of population. This company, however, is debarred from taking deposits or selling debentures; they are lending simply their own money. The committee has added certain provisions at the suggestion of the superintendent of loan companies. I might add that the whole proposition has been agreed to by the secretary of the loan association in Canada, and there is no objection from any quarter to this bill becoming law, the general desire being to prevent men and women from falling into the hands of loan sharks, who exact very high rates of interest and show very little mercy on the maturing of the debt. I make this explanation only because the sponsor of the bill was not a member of the committee. I repeat, the committee gave very careful consideration to this bill because it embodied a new departure in this country.

What did Mr. Finlayson
have to say about it?
He is quite in accord with the provisions of this bill, having gone into them all very carefully.

Did any official of the Finance department appear before the committee?

The Superintendent of Insurance appeared before the. committee, as well as the representative' of the loan companies, and everything was agreed to by all. the parties interested.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speechtext: I do not want to take up the time of the house, but it is perfectly understood and agreed that no member is committed to this bill by the mere fact that it gets its second reading. We simply want to send it to the committee to have it examined.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext: I do not think that this bill should be read the second time. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) is not here, and it is questionable whether the bill comes within the four corners of the jurisdiction of this parliament. It covers territory starting at Cornwall and going all the way into Quebec. The points presented in the bill have been sent by the cabinet to the supreme court for consideration and the question is to be heard within a few days. The bill involves a division of authority between the federal parliament and the provinces regarding international streams. This question was discussed a few years ago in reflation to the Morrisburg dam, and the matter of provincial rights then came under review. We have a series of documents and papers exchanged between the governments of the United States and of the Dominion of Canada touching the very points involved in this bill, and the moment we give the bill the second reading we automatically approve the principle of it. This, I submit, we have no right to do under the circumstances, especially in view of the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) some time ago that an opportunity would be afforded later on to discuss the whole question.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext: Let me assure my hon. friend, as I said in answer to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), that no hon. member is by any means committed to the principle of the bill in voting for the second reading of it. The sole purpose is to have the bill sent to the railway committee. I would not ask my hon. friend to commit himself to the principle of the bill. Indeed I am not committed to it myself, if it can be .proved that it is unsound.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext: Why do you not explain it?

subtopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext:
So far as I am concerned, I am opposed to sending the bill to any committee because it is altogether out of order in view of the fact that provincial Tights in the matter of water power are involved, and that this question has been referred to the supreme court. There is too much of this sort of thing in this house. Under the rules, the second reading of a bill approves the principle of it. This is in accordance with all the authorities-Bourinot, Beauchesne, May and others. This is a contentious stage of the bill, and especially a bill of this description.
I understand that a measure similar to this has passed the provincial legislature and this bill is now before parliament; we are asked to adopt concurrent legislation. And now the point is raised: What are the rights of the provinces and of the Dominion respectively in regard to the diversion from the river of water needed for navigation purposes? This question is among those referred to the supreme court, and it should not be discussed now, nor should the bill be sent to a committee of the house. This house has already dealt with questions similar to those involved in the bill. Such questions appear on the order paper, and it is not competent for us to forestall the action of parliament in the matter. The announcement has also been made that irrespective of the decision that will be rendered by the supreme court there is to be an appeal to the Privy Council on these various questions involved in the St. Lawrence waterway. This matter was under discussion the other day and the question came up in that connection as to whether these private bills should be passed. On April 10 the question was undeT consideration, and the very matters involved in the bill now before us were covered in the debate that then took place. That debate lasted one afternoon and the Prime Minister rose in his place and proposed an adjournment.
I would remind the house that the correspondence between the United States and the Dominion of Canda in regard to the St. Lawrence has been printed-500 copies in English and 200 in French. Various questions arise in these documents: What are the rights of the state of New York? What

Great Lakes and Power Company
are the rights of the province of Quebec in regard to the St. Lawrence, in so far as it lies exclusively in that province? What are the rights of the province of Ontario in relation to waters passing by its doors on their way to the St. Lawrence? And what are the international rights and the rights of this Dominion in respect of surplus water? There is a statute in this country known as The Navigable Waters Protection Act, which provides that before an application can be brought to parliament it shall be sent to the Minister of Public Works. Before any erection can be made on an international stream it must conform to the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Now, the preamble to this bill contains certain provisions which are hardly within the powers of this parliament, and it also raises the question of jurisdiction, which, I contend, is sub judice. Mr. Speaker has ruled upon this point; a similar question arose last session and, having been considered, the ruling was given.
I submit that this bill is out of order for the reasons I have indicated. I have here opinions from counsel for the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario of a few years ago, with regard! to this particular question, and there is no doubt, that the control of navigable water lies with the Dominion government. If it is desired to carry on any construction which will affect navigable waters application must be made to the Minister of Public Works, who holds a hearing and reports to the governor in council. These questions are now before the supreme court; counsel are acting for the Dominion government and for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; the pleadings are all in and a day has been named for the hearing. In view of that situation, how can we pass this bill?
Let us look at the preamble, which states:
Whereas a petition has been presented by the Great Lakes and Atlantic Canal and Power Company, Limited .... praying that it may be authorized to construct and operate a deep waterway from the western end of lake St. Francis at or near the town of Cornwall in the county of Stormont, in the province of Ontario to Hungry bay in the county of Beau-harnois in the province of Quebec, and to build a canal from said Hungry bay to a point at or near Melocheville, in the said county at lake St. Louis, and a deep waterway through lake St. Louis to a point at or near Caughna-waga in the county of La Prairie-[DOT]
They are not satisfied with that; they even name an alternative route. The canal system of this country, as I understand it, has been under the control of the Dominion government since about 1854, and since that
[Mr. Church.J
time we have spent over 8200,000,000 on that system. To-day we are spending large sums of money on the Welland canal, so I say we should not give a private company power to construct a canal of this kind. Here we have a canal to be built near the great port of Montreal, where we have spent so much money; we have the United States requesting permission to divert a great quantity of water to the Mississippi river through the Chicago drainage canal; they propose another canal from Ogdensburg to Albany, and if this sort of thing goes on there will not be a drop of water left in the port of Montreal. If this were purely a power company I would have no great objection to it; in Quebec they have a progressive premier who is always looking out for his province, but this is not such a company.
This bill gives this particular company the power to build a canal in the counties named, to the head of navigation, in and near the city of Montreal. It says:
so as to make and complete throughout the entire distance from Cornwall aforesaid to the harbour of Montreal as aforesaid, a navigable canal or canals.
This bill gives this particular company the power to build a private canal, because that is all it is going to be. It is going to be a private canal, and it is changing the whole canal policy of this country by handing it over to a private company, incorporated as it is in the province of Quebec, and giving this company powers in this province. You are going to upset the whole policy of canals in this country.
In 1854 the jurisdiction over these waters was in the Montreal harbour commission. They transferred the whole jurisdiction, in order to build a ship canal in 1854, from the port of Montreal to Quebec. The country spent $54,000,000 to dig that waterway. To hand over to this particular company the power to build this private canal, a private undertaking, as this preamble sets out, I must say is an entirely wrong principle.
